RagShortTexts: The House of Blois dominated the Loire valley, having supplied kings to England and counts.

Variants.Content: Blois and Chartres formed one of the oldest patrimonies in northern France, and its counts held court above the Loire. Stephen of Blois, a grandson of William the Conqueror through his mother Adela, took the English crown in 1135 and held it through civil war with the Empress Matilda. Although its lands broke up over generations, the family kept strategic tolls along the river and supported the Chartres cathedral works, which drew pilgrims from across Europe. Blois castellans watched river traffic closely, because every salt barge and timber raft paid tolls before it could pass the bridges.

Blois lay between Plantagenet Anjou and Capetian Paris, so its counts had to play both courts against each other. Each castellan kept veteran men-at-arms on the river crossings, and every fortified bridge gave the count a bargaining chip. A marriage alliance with one court could cost the goodwill of the other, so the envoys' letters were drafted with great care.

From the Blois ramparts, sentries watch barges hauling salt and timber up and down the Loire. Each evening a sergeant calls the watch, and the password changes with the moon. Patrols probe every cargo with iron spits, since smugglers hide wine casks under grain sacks to dodge the toll. A soldier who waves a barge past without a seal can lose a month's pay.
